papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.
bullets: Addresses the limits of transition-based objectives and trajectory generators for reasoning about complete paths.
Anchors an unknown stochastic action to a tractable reference process and learns a correction from trajectory comparisons.
Produces a differentiable path-space objective that captures local dynamics and nonadditive temporal dependencies.
Supports path ranking, mechanism steering, constrained optimization, and sampling using the same learned action.
Demonstrated across stochastic physical systems, orbital dynamics, and molecular simulations, including transfer across objectives and physical conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Recovering action and energy from trajectories is a latent-action world-model learning approach with transfer to dynamics modeling.
papers.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
papers.tldr: LEAP learns a reusable trajectory-level action from observed and reference paths, enabling inference, control, optimization, and sampling of dynamical systems.

papers.abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
bullets: Addresses the information bottleneck and limited performance of pooling- and projection-based sequence compression.
Computes regression coefficients in closed form during inference while learning the regression setup end-to-end with backpropagation.
Evaluated for block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging in multimodal large language models.
Achieves a large RULER improvement over attention-based compressors and matches an MLP merger using 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
Demonstrates test-time regression as a general compression primitive for efficient language and multimodal models.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time-regression sequence compression for sparse attention and visual token merging is an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
papers.tldr: TTR-Compressor uses differentiable test-time regression to turn input-token relationships into compact representations, improving sequence compression for language and multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of African scholarship in major pre-training datasets, especially for region-specific knowledge.
Aggregates 844,807 full-text papers from African journals, agricultural repositories, preprints, and publications by scholars at African institutions.
Covers scientific, medical, legal, agricultural, STEM/AI, and related domains across 31 African nations.
Provides layout-aware Markdown that preserves document structure, equations, and tables, with exact BPE token counts and an 8-domain taxonomy.
Released on Hugging Face to support continual pre-training and domain evaluation of foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Pan-African academic pretraining corpus is a language foundation-model resource.
papers.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
papers.tldr: Africa-Papers is an openly released 10.15-billion-token corpus designed to improve African representation in foundation-model pre-training across scientific and societal domains.

papers.abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.
bullets: Existing cosine-similarity selection over hidden states or gradients tends to select data tightly clustered around development examples.
ICLHerd uses a von Mises–Fisher kernel to balance selecting representative modes with averaging across broader data regions.
It uses in-context learning as an efficient proxy for tuning this trade-off during hyperparameter search.
Experiments report that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data-selection algorithms.
The approach focuses on selecting data aligned with targeted skills such as reasoning or multilinguality.
papers.selection_reason: LLM data-selection method with in-context learning as a proxy is relevant to language foundation-model development.
papers.title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
papers.tldr: ICLHerd improves LLM training-data selection by reducing the clustering bias of similarity-based methods through balanced mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and costly search in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation with learned policy proposals and value estimates.
Distills searched plans into the policy-value model through GPU-parallelized simulation.
The resulting model can act without simulator-based search at test time.
Outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines in simulated and real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon manipulation policy learned by distilling MCTS plans fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
papers.tldr: DISCO transfers long-horizon MCTS reasoning into a deployable policy for continuous-action multi-object rearrangement.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
bullets: Targets reflections, glare, motion-induced waterline shifts, and darkness that undermine RGB-based obstacle detection.
Fuses RGB, LWIR, FMCW mmWave radar, and inertial context, exposing calibrated bearing-sector obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status to navigation.
Distinguishes sensor dropout from valid obstacle-free observations, supporting predictable degradation during multimodal failures.
In eight held-out low-light recordings, calibrated fusion reached AP 0.869 and ECE 0.108; RGB alone had higher AP (0.903) when usable, while fusion preserved sensing when RGB failed.
A 24-leg, 351 m lake pilot included night operation using LWIR and radar without usable RGB; scope is limited to the reported lake recordings and pilot conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware multimodal obstacle perception and sensor-status modeling support autonomous surface vessel navigation.
papers.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
papers.tldr: A context-aware RGB-LWIR-radar fusion system helps resource-constrained ASVs maintain calibrated obstacle perception when RGB cameras degrade or fail, including at night.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become the backbone of a wide range of tasks, but their intensive computation and data movement incur substantial energy overhead. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) offers an energy-efficient alternative, yet its inherent hardware non-idealities perturb stored weights and can significantly degrade model performance. Although existing noise-aware training (NAT) methods improve robustness by injecting noise during training, they largely overlook the critical role of attention mechanisms in Transformer inference.To bridge this gap, we analyze how CIM-induced noise reshapes attention in Transformers and identify two key observations: (1) the divergence between clean and noisy attention maps increases substantially in deeper layers, and (2) conventional NAT can remain overconfident even when its attention routes deviate markedly from the clean reference. Motivated by these findings, we propose ABNAT, an attention-based noise-aware training framework that teaches the noisy student to preserve the clean teacher's headwise attention routes rather than merely reproduce answers, without hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants further reduce training cost.Extensive experiments across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers show that ABNAT consistently improves robustness over corresponding NAT baselines, improving noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reducing attention deviation by up to 85.77%.
bullets: Analog CIM hardware noise perturbs weights and can significantly degrade Transformer performance.
Noise causes increasing divergence between clean and noisy attention maps in deeper layers.
ABNAT uses clean-teacher, noisy-student training to align headwise attention routes, not just final predictions.
The framework requires no hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants reduce training cost.
Across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers, ABNAT improves noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reduces attention deviation by up to 85.77%.
papers.selection_reason: Attention-aware noise-aware training improves robustness of Transformers on energy-efficient analog compute-in-memory hardware.
papers.title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust Transformers on Analog Compute-in-Memory Systems
papers.tldr: ABNAT improves Transformer robustness to analog compute-in-memory noise by training noisy models to preserve clean attention routes.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
bullets: Addresses text-based communication bottlenecks and downstream prefill latency in multi-agent systems.
Combines an upstream model’s KV cache with a downstream model through linear interpolation, without fusion-adapter training.
Evaluated across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
Reports up to 8.6 percentage-point accuracy gains over single-model baselines.
Achieves up to 12.2× faster time to first token than text-based multi-model communication.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV-cache sharing between language models reduces latency and enables efficient latent LLM communication.
papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.tldr: CacheFuse enables training-free latent communication between heterogeneous language models by linearly interpolating their KV caches, improving accuracy while reducing communication latency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
bullets: State hallucination occurs when a VLA acts as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.
The failure is associated with reduced attention to task-relevant visual regions and activation of specific sparse autoencoder features.
SOUL unlearns hallucination-related policy knowledge while retaining features associated with successful behaviors.
Experiments across simulated and real-world settings and multiple VLA architectures reduce hallucinated failures and improve task success.
The approach is evaluated specifically for state hallucination and aims to preserve existing manipulation capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses state hallucination in vision-language-action robot policies using sparse-feature unlearning.
papers.title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: SOUL selectively removes sparse features linked to state hallucination in vision-language-action policies, reducing these failures while preserving manipulation ability.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of visual tokens, making long-form inference prohibitively expensive. While single-axis compression methods mitigate this, they hit a hard efficiency floor because they treat spatial and temporal redundancy independently. We present VETO (Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision-Language Models), a training-optional plug-in that eliminates this bottleneck through dual-axis compression: (i) an intra-frame compressor that merges semantically similar tokens within each frame via optimal-transport inspired matching, and (ii) an inter-frame compressor that identifies and merges temporally redundant frames. The key design insight is hierarchical ordering: by first compressing spatial dimensions, VETO drastically reduces the cost of subsequent global temporal matching, bypassing the efficiency wall of single-axis approaches, with an advantage that grows with modern fully-fused attention infrastructure. Empirically, VETO achieves up to 45% faster inference (e.g., on LLaVA-OneVision-7B) while preserving or improving accuracy. Under extreme token starvation (10% budget), VETO outperforms VFlowOpt (54.9%), VisionZip (52.6%), and FastV (47.9%) with 55.7% accuracy. We demonstrate universal applicability across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA, with zero-shot accuracy preserved or improved in all cases.
bullets: Targets the quadratic visual-token cost that makes long-form video inference expensive.
Uses a training-optional dual-axis plug-in: optimal-transport-inspired intra-frame token merging followed by inter-frame redundant-frame merging.
Hierarchical ordering makes global temporal matching cheaper by first reducing spatial tokens.
Achieves up to 45% faster inference and maintains or improves zero-shot accuracy across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA.
At a 10% token budget, reaches 55.7% accuracy, exceeding the cited VFlowOpt, VisionZip, and FastV results.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-axis spatial and temporal token compression directly targets efficient long-video VLM inference.
papers.title: VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: VETO accelerates long-video VLM inference by hierarchically compressing redundant spatial and temporal visual tokens while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Financial forecasting from earnings conference calls requires models to reason over complex corporate disclosures, market expectations, and subtle communication signals. However, existing financial benchmarks are often limited to unimodal inputs or single-task settings, making it difficult to evaluate whether multimodal large language models (LLMs) can support real-world financial analysis. In this paper, we introduce MM-FinEval, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal LLMs across multiple financial tasks. MM-FinEval spans a diverse timeline from 2019 to 2022. The entire proposed dataset contains 2,045 S\&P 500 conference earning calls as inputs and 12 financial task labels as outputs. Each input contains three modalities: a word-to-word text transcript of the earning call, the corresponding presentation slides used during the call, and the entire audio recording. To establish a rigorous evaluation framework, we analyze 19 baseline models across three distinct model categories: Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations. We observe that small-size Any-to-Any models processing all three modalities achieve strong performance, even when compared against larger proprietary models restricted to two-modality inputs. This indicates that our tri-modal dataset design introduces useful, non-redundant information. These results validate that text, audio, and visual data serve as important, complementary signals that mimic the decision-making process of expert human analysts.
bullets: Covers 2,045 S&P 500 earnings calls from 2019–2022 with 12 financial task labels.
Each example combines transcript text, presentation slides, and full audio recordings.
Evaluates 19 baseline models across Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations.
Small Any-to-Any models using all three modalities perform strongly relative to larger proprietary models using only two.
Results suggest that text, audio, and visual signals provide complementary information for financial analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating multimodal LLMs across text, audio, and visual inputs fits the multimodal foundation models scope.
papers.title: MM-FinEval: A Multi-Task Multimodal Benchmark for Real-World Financial Forecasting
papers.tldr: MM-FinEval is a tri-modal, multi-task benchmark for testing multimodal LLMs on realistic financial forecasting from earnings calls.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance, AI agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments to tackle complex sequential tasks (e.g., document processing, cross-application collaboration), relying heavily on actions ranging from GUI operations to semantic APIs. However, three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates or outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos. To address these, we propose AnyAct, a universal action layer that unifies available capabilities into a self-evolving action space, enabling agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems. AnyAct's core design focuses on two objectives: constructing this action space via hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions), and enabling reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module that unifies multi-modal feedback. Additionally, it defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for a balance between task success rate and execution cost. Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark we developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial performance gains over baseline methods across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench and improvements are particularly notable for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, which is half the steps required by most competitors.
bullets: Addresses tool-scale limits, changing tool reliability, and incompatible feedback across GUI, API, visual, textual, and structured interfaces.
Builds a self-evolving action space using hierarchical progressive retrieval and test-time pruning of unreliable actions.
Combines primitive and semantic actions with heterogeneous observation grounding for reliability-aware orchestration.
Balances task success with execution cost in dynamic, multi-tool environments.
Reports state-of-the-art results on LiveMCPBench and 77.27% success on OSMCP using 50 steps, notably benefiting models with limited native capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving action space with test-time reliability pruning is transferable to deployment-time adaptation for agents.
papers.title: AnyAct: Universal Action for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.tldr: AnyAct helps LLM agents act reliably in large, changing tool ecosystems by dynamically selecting, evaluating, and coordinating heterogeneous actions.

papers.abstract: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.
bullets: Addresses the expert effort required to design mode-switching controllers (MSCs) for tasks with varying sensory and compute demands.
Represents MSCs as interpretable programs and iteratively refines their modes, resource allocations, and transitions.
Evaluates candidate designs with MSC-compatible controller synthesis, including reinforcement learning in simulation.
Experiments across diverse control benchmarks show LEMCA surpasses monolithic designs’ Pareto frontier by reclaiming resources during easier phases.
Provides an automated, low-effort approach for synthesizing efficient MSC architectures.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided evolutionary synthesis of mode-switching robot controllers that reduce resource use; relevant to robot control and efficient AI.
papers.title: LEMCA: LLM-Guided Synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures
papers.tldr: LEMCA uses LLM-guided evolutionary program synthesis to automatically design resource-efficient robot controllers that switch modes as task difficulty changes.

papers.abstract: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting schematic map geometry with a robot’s first-person visual navigation.
RouteScribe separates route inference from verbalization by generating an explicit map-coordinate route scaffold before producing instructions.
Uses start–goal line conditional flow matching to deform a straight waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route.
Real-world experiments report higher success rate and SPL than direct generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source flow matching.
The modular design keeps maps and scaffolds upstream, enabling executor replacement without retraining map-to-language modules.
papers.selection_reason: Map-based route scaffolding converted into instructions for a pretrained VLN policy; directly addresses vision-language navigation.
papers.title: NaViRrator: Robot Navigation from Human-Readable Maps through a Learned Visual Route
papers.tldr: NaViRRator converts human-readable map destinations into route-grounded language instructions that pretrained vision-language navigation policies can execute from egocentric observations.

papers.abstract: Although conventional controllers and disturbance observers (DOBs) are the standard for precision tracking in manipulators, they suffer from parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. This study proposes a residual reinforcement learning DOB framework that pairs an analytical observer with an RL policy. The deterministic baseline operates within a reliable region, whereas the RL policy explicitly targets the residuals that the model cannot capture. To make this compensation disturbance-aware, an estimator network aligns the observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime and enabling rapid adaptation across disturbance transitions. To guarantee stability, we derived and enforced a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis such that the closed loop provably confines the tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs. Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrated consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance that was not observed during training.
bullets: Combines an analytical disturbance observer with RL that learns only unmodeled residual dynamics.
Uses a disturbance-aware estimator to organize latent representations by disturbance regime and adapt across transitions.
Derives an ISS-based, state-dependent action bound that guarantees the closed-loop tracking error remains within a certified envelope.
On a 6-DOF manipulator, reduced tracking error by 27.8% in zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and 38.0% under unseen base vibration.
papers.selection_reason: Residual reinforcement learning for manipulator disturbance compensation with stability-certified action bounds; relevant to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Stability-aware Residual Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robotic Manipulator Disturbance Compensation
papers.tldr: A stability-constrained residual RL observer improves robotic-manipulator disturbance compensation while preserving a provable tracking-error bound.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.
bullets: Addresses safe aerial navigation when accurate ground-truth obstacle data is unavailable.
Uses a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to encode detailed scene geometry.
Introduces a reachability-based planner exploiting quadrotor differential flatness.
Computes continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate vehicle occupancy.
Finds paths in 81.2% of challenging test cases, compared with 51.2% for the nearest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Risk-aware quadrotor motion planning using a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation; relevant to robot navigation and 3D scene modeling.
papers.title: AirSplan: Risk-Aware Motion Planning for Quadrotors in Cluttered 3D Gaussian Splats
papers.tldr: AirSplan combines high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting with risk-aware reachability planning to find collision-free quadrotor paths in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance in diverse generative robot policies.
Optimizes policy input noise while evaluating constraints on the resulting state trajectory, preserving the policy’s behavior space.
Uses distribution-consistency regularization and online population-based particle optimization.
Evaluated on state-, image-, and vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial.
Improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while achieving lower runtime than gradient-guided generation.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of one-step generative robot policies via noise-space trajectory optimization; applies to VLA policies and manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Safe Real-Time Policy Steering via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization for One-Step Generative Policies
papers.tldr: INSPO enables real-time constraint-aware steering of one-step generative robot policies by optimizing their input noise instead of repeatedly modifying actions or generation steps.

papers.abstract: Collision-free motion planning requires reliable collision models from sensed environments and validation of states along a continuous trajectory. To make this tractable, most planners check for collision at discrete states along continuous trajectories against a single determinized model of the environment, introducing a trade-off between safety and computational efficiency. While continuous collision checking approaches that approximate the swept volume of the robot exist, they are computationally expensive or overly conservative. Data-driven approaches can learn the swept volume; however, these neural models are susceptible to approximation errors and are therefore often limited to serving as coarse filters for downstream collision checkers. In this work, we propose to learn a signed distance function of the swept volume as a probabilistic field, enabling quantification of epistemic uncertainty, incorporation of perception noise, and eventual integration into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework. We demonstrate our approach on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.
bullets: Addresses the safety–efficiency trade-off of discrete collision checks and costly or conservative continuous swept-volume approximations.
Learns the swept volume as a probabilistic signed distance field rather than a deterministic neural approximation.
Models epistemic uncertainty and incorporates perception noise for more reliable collision reasoning.
Targets integration with chance-constrained trajectory optimization.
Demonstrated on high-dimensional manipulation tasks in simulation and on real hardware with significant sensor noise.
papers.selection_reason: Learned probabilistic swept-volume signed distance field for chance-constrained trajectory optimization; relevant to learned planning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Stochastic Neural Signed Swept Volume for Real-time Chance-Constrained Trajectory Optimization
papers.tldr: A probabilistic neural signed-distance model of robot swept volumes enables uncertainty-aware, chance-constrained trajectory optimization under noisy perception.

papers.abstract: Audio large language models (AudioLLMs) operate reactively, responding only when queried. We introduce proactive audio assistance, where an AudioLLM monitors an audio stream and autonomously decides when to alert the user from a single natural-language intent, motivated by wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users. We propose Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: \texttt{<interrupt>} and \texttt{<silent>}, capturing four states: onset detection, sustained-relevance triggering, irrelevance suppression, and de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, ISM achieves 99.6\% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio, ISM achieves the highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training, the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.
bullets: Addresses the reactive nature of AudioLLMs, with potential wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users.
Uses two special decoding tokens—<interrupt> and <silent>—to model onset detection, sustained relevance, suppression, and de-duplication.
Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, it achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50.
On noisy kitchen audio, it maintains strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression and requires no domain-specific training.
Streaming evaluation indicates real-time feasibility with 3.5-second average latency.
papers.selection_reason: Extends an audio LLM with proactive interrupt/silent decoding, fitting multimodal large language model research.
papers.title: I'll Keep an Ear Out: Teaching AudioLLMs Proactive Audio Assistance
papers.tldr: ISM enables AudioLLMs to proactively monitor audio and alert users at the right moments without explicit queries.

papers.abstract: Multi-party human-robot collaboration poses a dual challenge: robot decisions should remain interpretable and auditable, while executed actions must satisfy safety constraints during physical interaction. Combining explainable decision-tree policies with control-barrier-function (CBF) filtering provides a promising architecture but creates two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Safety projection changes the action applied to the environment, while the coupled proposal graph can misalign independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update. We present safety-aligned gradient enforcement (SAGE) to address both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity to internalize repeatedly active safety constraints. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieves a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show that direct CBF filtering reduces collision frequency by 98.5% but decreases success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.
bullets: Addresses two mismatches: CBF safety projection changes executed actions, and independently learned actors can diverge from team-level updates.
SAIL uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map for learning while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program during execution.
TALO provides a team-aware reference and Lyapunov correction to regulate independent actor updates.
In nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieved 71.0% success with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps.
Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrated deployment feasibility; ablations reduced proposal violations and update inconsistency.
papers.selection_reason: Safety-aligned multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-robot collaboration directly fits learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: SAGE: Safety-Aligned Gradient Enforcement for Human--Robot Collaboration
papers.tldr: SAGE aligns multi-agent learning with safety-filtered execution and team objectives for interpretable, safer human–robot collaboration.

papers.abstract: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.
bullets: Addresses cooperative referring scene understanding when targets or landmarks originate from another agent’s observations.
Builds local open-vocabulary, instance-aware Gaussian maps and aligns them using geometric and semantic consistency.
Uses a view-conditioned mask relation graph to reason about spatial relationships from the querying robot’s viewpoint.
Introduces CoQuad-Ref, a real-world and simulated indoor benchmark.
Refinement reduces simulated rotation error from 2.58° to 0.15°, while real-world referring mIoU improves from 52.6% to 68.8% over ReferSplat.
papers.selection_reason: View-conditioned referring grounding over fused 3D Gaussian maps is a strong spatial-intelligence and embodied perception contribution.
papers.title: CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding
papers.tldr: CoRef-GS enables viewpoint-aware language grounding across independently built Gaussian maps by jointly aligning their geometry and semantics.

papers.abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.
bullets: Uses 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and hand-object interaction data for supervision.
Introduces TwinTouch-20H, 20 hours of generated paired data that converts gloved views into bare-hand appearances while preserving tactile labels.
Predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos.
Outperforms prior contact-prediction methods on OakInk2 and qualitatively generalizes to unseen natural bare-hand videos.
Performance improves with more glove supervision, eliminating the need for tactile instrumentation during video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts dense tactile/contact forces from egocentric human-object videos, directly supporting dexterous manipulation skill learning.
papers.title: TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation
papers.tldr: TouchSight predicts dense full-hand contact forces from egocentric video alone by using generatively augmented glove recordings to bridge the gap to bare-hand interactions.

papers.abstract: The symbiotic scaling of artificial intelligence models and high-performance computing systems continually creates algorithmic challenges in their convergence. Foundation models (FMs) are a crucial example, requiring months-long training on thousands of cutting-edge GPUs. Sharded data parallelism (DP) is the dominant strategy to accelerate such computations by splitting data and models across multiple GPUs. However, it incurs prohibitive communication overhead when deployed at scale, particularly on multi-tier interconnects with heterogeneous performance. Inspired by the efficient communication principles of federated learning (FL), this work introduces two hybrid algorithms - FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP - interleaving sharded DP with FedAvg-style aggregations. Such approaches decouple large DP deployments into smaller, loosely-coupled federation groups, requiring minimal inter-group traffic while keeping the global batch size bounded by the groups' size. Formal analysis of communication costs and experimental validation prove their scalability and flexibility. A Llama3.1 8B pre-training on 512 A100 GPUs shows that, under identical hyperparameters, FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP achieve up to 8.04 faster data processing and 4.48 lower evaluation perplexity than their counterparts, demonstrating superior computational efficiency and improved model quality. These properties stem from reduced communication overhead and the bounded growth of the global batch size relative to the federation group size.
bullets: Addresses prohibitive communication overhead in sharded data parallelism across heterogeneous, multi-tier GPU interconnects.
Introduces FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP, which combine sharded data parallelism with FedAvg-style aggregation across loosely coupled federation groups.
Keeps global batch-size growth bounded by federation-group size while minimizing inter-group traffic.
On Llama3.1 8B pre-training with 512 A100 GPUs, the methods achieved up to 8.04× faster data processing and 4.48× lower evaluation perplexity under identical hyperparameters.
Validated through communication-cost analysis and experiments, with scope focused on large-scale foundation-model training.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces communication overhead and accelerates large-scale model training, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: Accelerating Sharded Data Parallelism at Scale with Federated Learning
papers.tldr: FL-inspired hybrid sharded data-parallel algorithms reduce cross-group communication while improving training throughput and model quality at scale.
